title: Iran Sends Top Official to Pakistan With Message for Khamenei as US Strikes Enter 10th Day
excerpt: Iran's Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni met Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and PM Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad on Tuesday, seeking to revive the collapsed US-Iran ceasefire as fighting intensifies across the Gulf.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Iran's Interior Minister met Pakistan's leaders to discuss reviving a collapsed US-Iran ceasefire.
  • US-Iran military strikes continue for the 10th day, escalating tensions in the Gulf region.
  • Oil prices surged to nearly $90 a barrel amid ongoing conflict and shipping disruptions.
  • Iran and Pakistan aim to boost bilateral trade from $3 billion to $10 billion annually.

Momeni's Mission in Islamabad

Iran's Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni arrived in Islamabad on Monday night and held back-to-back meetings with Pakistan's most powerful military and civilian leaders on Tuesday, according to Dawn and the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

https://x.com/PakPMO/status/2079580192826409455

Momeni first met Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, where the two discussed regional security, bilateral relations, and effective border management. The Iranian minister "appreciated Pakistan's consistent efforts and its diplomatic role in easing regional tensions," the ISPR said.

He then met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at the PM House. Sharif expressed deep concern over the escalation in the Gulf and reiterated Pakistan's willingness to mediate between Washington and Tehran.

"Pakistan would continue to play its role as an honest and sincere mediator and facilitator."

— PM Shehbaz Sharif, official press release

He then met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at the PM House."**

"The Iranian minister "appreciated Pakistan's consistent efforts and its diplomatic role in easing regional tensions," the ISPR said.</p> <p>He then met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at the PM House."

The visit follows an established pattern. In June, Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had traveled to Tehran carrying what he described as a "special message" from Munir and Sharif to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei. That message addressed the ceasefire negotiations. Tuesday's meeting reversed the direction, with Iran's envoy now delivering Tehran's position to Islamabad.

A Ceasefire in Tatters

The diplomatic push comes against a backdrop of intensifying violence. The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, signed in June between the US and Iran with Pakistan's help, was meant to end hostilities that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February. But the deal collapsed within weeks.

US forces have conducted airstrikes on Iranian military targets for 10 consecutive nights, hitting command centres, missile launch sites, and air defence systems across multiple provinces, according to US Central Command. Iran has responded by attacking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz — on Tuesday alone, it forced the crew of a tanker to abandon ship — and launching drones and missiles at US-allied states including Jordan and Bahrain.

President Donald Trump warned on social media Monday: "Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!" His Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, said Monday that the two countries are now in a "full-scale war."

Oil prices have climbed sharply. Brent crude traded at nearly $90 a barrel on Tuesday, and regular gasoline in the US reached an average of $4 a gallon, according to the Associated Press. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global crude oil once transited, has slowed to a crawl — Lloyd's List Intelligence reported only three ships passed through on Sunday.

India's Stakes in the Corridor

The escalation has direct consequences for India and its diaspora. India imported roughly 15 percent of its crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict disrupted traffic. Rising oil prices feed directly into inflation, affecting food and fuel costs for India's 1.4 billion people.

For Indian expatriates in the Gulf — an estimated 9 million across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Oman — the widening conflict zone raises safety concerns. Bahrain, home to a significant Indian community and the US Navy's 5th Fleet, sounded missile alert sirens on Tuesday after another Iranian barrage.

Pakistan's mediator role also carries implications for India-Pakistan dynamics. Islamabad's growing diplomatic stature as a broker between Washington and Tehran contrasts with its strained relations with New Delhi, and any eventual deal could reshape regional power alignments.

Trade Ambitions Amid the Chaos

Beyond the ceasefire talks, Momeni discussed expanding Pakistan-Iran bilateral trade from $3 billion to $10 billion annually. He told Iran's Mehr news agency that achieving the target would require "around 2,000 trucks or containers crossing between the two countries daily," compared to about 20 percent of that capacity currently in use.

The two nations also revisited the long-delayed Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline. Pakistan and Iran share a 900-kilometre border and maintain close historical, cultural, and religious links, though the relationship has been periodically tested by cross-border militant activity.

What Comes Next

A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran has received a proposal from mediators for a 10-day ceasefire. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Washington remains "committed to diplomacy" but doubts Tehran's sincerity. Whether Momeni's visit produces a concrete opening or amounts to another round of fruitless shuttle diplomacy may become clear in the coming days.
